{"id": "1c3c7efe-2cad-4318-ab25-df25f5243776", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_s4VqvcsYqHw8mm1Sa81l2X", "content": "[{'text': '{\"content\": \"---\\\\nname: network-log-analyzer\\\\ndescription: \\'Use this skill when a user is troubleshooting AWS network connectivity: a connection times out, is refused, or resets; traffic flows only one way; flow logs show REJECT and they need to know whether a security group or network ACL caused it; TCP handshakes fail; transfers are slow or retransmit; large packets hang; idle connections drop; DNS queries time out; or they want top talkers or the real source behind a NAT gateway or EKS pod. Also use it whenever the user shares VPC Flow Logs, a packet capture, or tcpdump, Wireshark, or tshark output, even if they don\\'\\'t name the problem.\\'\\\\nmetadata:\\\\n  version: \\\\\"1.0.0\\\\\"\\\\n  author: midakin\\\\n  summary: \\\\\"Troubleshoots connectivity from VPC Flow Logs and packet captures: SG vs NACL rejects, TCP handshake and retransmission analysis, MTU, idle resets, DNS.\\\\\"\\\\n  aws-devops-agent-skills.agent-types: \\\\\"CHAT, INCIDENT_RCA\\\\\"\\\\n  aws-devops-agent-skills.aws-services: \\\\\"Amazon VPC, Amazon EC2, Amazon CloudWatch, Amazon S3\\\\\"\\\\n  aws-devops-agent-skills.technical-domains: \\\\\"Networking, Observability\\\\\"\\\\n---\\\\n\\\\n# Network Log Analyzer\\\\n\\\\nTurn network evidence into a diagnosis. There are two kinds of evidence:\\\\n\\\\n- **VPC Flow Logs**: what each ENI allowed or rejected per aggregation interval. Query them in\\\\n  CloudWatch Logs or Athena, or read an export the user attaches.\\\\n- **Packet captures**: what actually crossed the wire at one point. You can\\'t read binary\\\\n  pcap/pcapng, and chat doesn\\'t accept them, so the user converts them to text with tshark or\\\\n  tcpdump first.\\\\n\\\\nThis skill is **read-only**. It never changes security groups, network ACLs, routes, flow logs,\\\\nor mirroring sessions.\\\\n\\\\n## Verification rules (mandatory)\\\\n\\\\n- Base every finding on evidence actually present in query results or attached files. Label\\\\n  each one **Observed** (directly in the data), **Inferred** (follows from documented AWS or\\\\n  Wireshark behavior), or **[Heuristic]** (analysis judgment).\\\\n- State assumptions before answering: the **capture point**, the **flow log format** (which\\\\n  fields exist), and the **time window** (UTC).\\\\n- Check AWS and Wireshark behavior against the reference files. If you can\\'t verify a claim,\\\\n  say \\\\\"I cannot verify this\\\\\". Only cite URLs listed in the reference files or retrieved during\\\\n  the task.\\\\n- When the evidence isn\\'t Wireshark output, anything you say Wireshark *would* flag, and any value\\\\n  you derive from a pattern (such as the IP ID of an unseen packet), is **Inferred**, not Observed.\\\\n\\\\n## Workflow\\\\n\\\\nCopy this checklist into your working notes and tick each step. Each step depends on the one\\\\nbefore it.\\\\n\\\\n- [ ] Step 1: Classify the evidence path (A, B, or both)\\\\n- [ ] Step 2A or 2B: Collect scoped evidence\\\\n- [ ] Step 3: Interpret it with documented behavior\\\\n- [ ] Step 4: Confirm with read-only checks\\\\n- [ ] Step 5: Self-check the findings, then answer in the output format\\\\n\\\\n## Step 1: Classify the evidence path\\\\n\\\\nDecide which path applies before collecting anything:\\\\n\\\\n- **Path A: flow logs reachable in the account.** CloudWatch Logs or S3 with Athena are\\\\n  available to you. Query them directly (Step 2A).\\\\n- **Path B: the user has or must provide evidence.** The flow logs aren\\'t queryable from here,\\\\n  or the evidence is a packet capture (Step 2B).\\\\n- **Both**, when a capture exists alongside flow logs. Flow logs show allow and reject per ENI.\\\\n  The capture shows what happened on the wire.\\\\n\\\\nIf the symptom, endpoints (IPs, ports, protocol) or time window are missing, ask for them\\\\nfirst. Don\\'t start broad unscoped queries.\\\\n\\\\n## Step 2A: Query flow logs\\\\n\\\\n1. Get the format:\\\\n   `aws ec2 describe-flow-logs --filter Name=resource-id,Values=<vpc|subnet|eni>`. Read\\\\n   `LogFormat` and `LogDestination`. The default v2 format has no `tcp-flags` or\\\\n   `flow-direction`. An existing flow log\\'s format can\\'t be changed: to add fields, the user\\\\n   creates a new flow log (suggest it; don\\'t create it).\\\\n2. Load [references/flow-log-queries.md](references/flow-log-queries.md) and run its scoped\\\\n   queries: rejected flows, both directions between the two hosts, and gaps (`logStatus`).\\\\n   **Always time-box them**, because Logs Insights and Athena bill by data scanned. Custom\\\\n   formats need `parse @message` in the exact field order.\\\\n3. For record-level pairing, pull only the failing conversation\\'s records\\\\n   (`filter-log-events` with the host as the filter pattern).\\\\n\\\\n## Step 2B: Get evidence from the user\\\\n\\\\nLoad [references/preparing-evidence.md](references/preparing-evidence.md). Paste its exact\\\\ncommands into your reply, and ask for the files in its \\\\\"What to send\\\\\" tables. Never refer the\\\\nuser to the skill\\'s own files by name, because they can\\'t see them:\\\\n\\\\n- **Flow logs:** `LogFormat`, a rejects aggregate (CSV), and the raw records for the failing\\\\n  conversation, from both ENIs if possible.\\\\n- **Captures:** the tshark overview, the header-only problem-packet CSV, and the handshake CSV.\\\\n  Ask for the **capture point**, the capture filter, the snaplen, and whether offload was on.\\\\n- Ask for **headers only, never payloads**. Attachments are visible to everyone in the Agent\\\\n  Space.\\\\n\\\\n## Step 3: Interpret with documented behavior\\\\n\\\\n**Flow logs.** Load [references/vpc-flow-logs.md](references/vpc-flow-logs.md) to interpret\\\\nany flow log record. It holds the field definitions, flag values, address translation, and\\\\ntraffic that isn\\'t logged. The core rules:\\\\n\\\\n- Request ACCEPT plus response REJECT on the same ENI points to a **network ACL** (NACLs are\\\\n  stateless; SGs are stateful).\\\\n- A lone REJECT with no reverse traffic could be **the SG or the NACL**. Flow logs can\\'t tell\\\\n  which: check the SG first, then the NACL. Never claim certainty, and don\\'t call either one\\\\n  \\\\\"more likely\\\\\" without configuration evidence.\\\\n- `tcp-flags` are OR-ed per record, so match the bit, not one exact value. Pair each SYN with\\\\n  what came back: SYN-ACK means answered, RST means refused, nothing means dropped downstream.\\\\n- Some traffic is **not logged**, and SKIPDATA intervals hide flows, so a missing record isn\\'t\\\\n  proof that traffic didn\\'t happen.\\\\n- Behind a NAT gateway or EKS pod, the real source is in specific legs and fields. Check the\\\\n  address translation section before naming a source. If the format lacks the `pkt-*` fields,\\\\n  say so: an existing flow log\\'s format can\\'t be changed, so adding them takes a new flow log.\\\\n\\\\n**Captures.** Load [references/wireshark-analysis.md](references/wireshark-analysis.md) to read\\\\nany tshark or tcpdump output (flag definitions, precedence, capture point, artifacts). Load\\\\n[references/packet-capture-analysis.md](references/packet-capture-analysis.md) for TCP\\\\nsignatures, MTU values, and ENA counters. The core rules:\\\\n\\\\n- **Fix the capture point first** from the handshake timing split.\\\\n- Use Wireshark\\'s `tcp.analysis.*` vocabulary. Flags overlap, so separate spurious\\\\n  retransmissions and capture gaps from real loss. Expert Info is a hint, not a verdict.\\\\n- Offload (TSO/GRO) makes packet sizes meaningless for MTU diagnosis in that capture.\\\\n- SGs and NACLs **drop silently**. An RST or ICMP error comes from a host, firewall, or router.\\\\n- **No loss isn\\'t the same as healthy.** A window-limited flow shows no retransmissions.\\\\n- **Resets after an idle gap** point to an idle timeout (load balancer or connection\\\\n  tracking). Always recommend the fix: TCP keepalives, or connection-pool idle limits, shorter\\\\n  than that timeout.\\\\n\\\\n**Symptoms.** Load\\\\n[references/troubleshooting-playbooks.md](references/troubleshooting-playbooks.md) when the\\\\nsymptom is a timeout, refusal, one-way traffic, slow transfer, large packets hanging, idle\\\\nresets, DNS, or a NAT/EKS source question. It maps each to evidence, causes, and confirmation,\\\\nincluding the MTU and idle-timeout values to compare against.\\\\n\\\\n## Step 4: Confirm with read-only checks\\\\n\\\\nValidate the suspected cause against configuration using read-only calls only (`describe-*`,\\\\n`get-*`, `list-*`, `search-*`). For example: `ec2 describe-security-groups`,\\\\n`describe-network-acls`, `describe-route-tables`, `describe-network-interfaces`,\\\\n`describe-flow-logs`, `describe-nat-gateways`, `describe-instances`,\\\\n`search-transit-gateway-routes`, `elbv2 describe-listener-attributes`,\\\\n`cloudwatch get-metric-data`, and `cloudtrail lookup-events` (recent changes). Reachability\\\\nAnalyzer and Traffic Mirroring create resources: suggest them, but don\\'t create them.\\\\n\\\\nAlways write the read-only commands out in your answer, with the IDs or filters to use. Do this\\\\neven when you ran them yourself, or when the resource isn\\'t in the account you can reach, so\\\\nthe user can repeat the check.\\\\n\\\\nFor why a route was chosen (TGW, Cloud WAN, Direct Connect path selection), use the\\\\n`aws-routing` skill if it\\'s available. For live VPC resolver probing, use\\\\n`aws-vpc-dns-investigation` if it\\'s available.\\\\n\\\\n## Step 5: Self-check before answering\\\\n\\\\nCheck each finding before you present it, and fix it if any check fails:\\\\n\\\\n- [ ] Every Observed finding points at a specific record, query result, or frame you actually\\\\n  have. If it doesn\\'t, relabel it Inferred or drop it.\\\\n- [ ] Counts come from aggregates (Logs Insights or Athena results, tshark `-z` statistics), not\\\\n  hand-tallied rows. If a figure was read from rows, say so and mark it approximate.\\\\n- [ ] Every AWS or Wireshark behavior you state matches the reference file you loaded. If it\\\\n  isn\\'t there and you didn\\'t retrieve a source, say \\\\\"I cannot verify this\\\\\".\\\\n- [ ] Each query or display filter you show would reproduce the finding on the user\\'s data.\\\\n- [ ] Every command you suggest running is read-only.\\\\n\\\\n## Output requirements\\\\n\\\\n**Compact form (the default for conceptual questions).** If the question has no evidence files\\\\nand no account data, answer in under about 200 words: the answer, its evidence label, one\\\\nread-only check, and the main coverage gap.\\\\n\\\\n**Full form**, when there\\'s evidence or account data to analyze. Every response must include:\\\\n\\\\n1. **Assumptions:** capture point, flow log format and fields, time window, filters applied.\\\\n2. **Findings**, most severe first. Each one has its evidence (ENI and time, or file, frame\\\\n   and stream), a Wireshark display filter or query that reproduces it, and a label:\\\\n   Observed, Inferred, or [Heuristic]. List what the evidence or the user\\'s description directly\\\\n   shows as separate **Observed** findings, before any Inferred or [Heuristic] finding that\\\\n   interprets them.\\\\n3. **Coverage gaps:** SKIPDATA, traffic that isn\\'t logged, missing fields, one-sided or\\\\n   truncated captures, and anything outside the exported slice.\\\\n4. **Most likely root cause**, and what evidence would disprove it.\\\\n5. **Read-only confirmation commands.**\\\\n6. **Recommended fix** (described, never applied), with blast radius and rollback. Describe\\\\n   rollback in words. If you show a command, label it **mutating, for the change record, not to\\\\n   run now**. Recommend testing in non-production first. Investigations need this too: not\\\\n   applying a fix doesn\\'t mean not recommending one.\\\\n\\\\n## What this skill does NOT do\\\\n\\\\n- Modify any AWS resource, or run mutating commands.\\\\n- Read binary capture files, or ask for packet payloads.\\\\n- Prove a negative from incomplete evidence.\\\\n\\\\n## References\\\\n\\\\nLoad each file only when its condition applies:\\\\n\\\\n- [references/vpc-flow-logs.md](references/vpc-flow-logs.md): when interpreting any flow log\\\\n  record (fields v2 to v11, SG vs NACL inference, tcp-flags, address translation, unlogged\\\\n  traffic)\\\\n- [references/flow-log-queries.md](references/flow-log-queries.md): when querying flow logs in\\\\n  CloudWatch Logs Insights or Athena\\\\n- [references/preparing-evidence.md](references/preparing-evidence.md): when the user has to\\\\n  export flow logs or convert a capture to text\\\\n- [references/wireshark-analysis.md](references/wireshark-analysis.md): when reading tshark or\\\\n  tcpdump output (tcp.analysis definitions and precedence, completeness, artifacts, filters)\\\\n- [references/packet-capture-analysis.md](references/packet-capture-analysis.md): when planning\\\\n  a capture (EC2, Windows, EKS, Traffic Mirroring) or matching TCP signatures, MTU, ENA counters\\\\n- [references/troubleshooting-playbooks.md](references/troubleshooting-playbooks.md): when\\\\n  mapping a symptom to evidence, causes, and confirmation\\\\n\", \"resource_manifest\": [\"SKILL.md\", \"references/flow-log-queries.md\", \"references/packet-capture-analysis.md\", \"references/preparing-evidence.md\", \"references/troubleshooting-playbooks.md\", \"references/vpc-flow-logs.md\", \"references/wireshark-analysis.md\"]}'}]", "status": "success", "type": "tool_result"}], "created_at": null}

{"id": "bbfbf027-9a0e-46ee-938b-ca34b1d280a7", "role": "user", "content": [{"id": "tooluse_iL73xo8xUeXjAEfoq0gwOK", "content": "[{'text': '# Wireshark / tshark Expert Analysis\\n\\nHow to analyze a capture the way an experienced Wireshark analyst does: method first, then\\nWireshark\\'s own TCP analysis, filters, and statistics. Behavior and field names come from the\\nWireshark sources listed below (field names checked against the 4.6.x display-filter\\nreference). Items marked **[Not verified this session]** are standard practice that I couldn\\'t\\nconfirm against a fetched source. Confirm them on the installed version before relying on them.\\n\\n## Sources (retrieved and used)\\n\\n- [User\\'s Guide 7.5: TCP Analysis](https://www.wireshark.org/docs/wsug_html_chunked/ChAdvTCPAnalysis.html): flag definitions, precedence, completeness\\n- [User\\'s Guide 7.4: Expert Information](https://www.wireshark.org/docs/wsug_html_chunked/ChAdvExpert.html)\\n- [User\\'s Guide 6.4: Building Display Filter Expressions](https://www.wireshark.org/docs/wsug_html_chunked/ChWorkBuildDisplayFilterSection.html)\\n- [User\\'s Guide 11.5: Decode As](https://www.wireshark.org/docs/wsug_html_chunked/ChCustProtocolDissectionSection.html)\\n- [tshark(1) man page](https://www.wireshark.org/docs/man-pages/tshark.html)\\n- Display filter reference: [tcp](https://www.wireshark.org/docs/dfref/t/tcp.html), [ip](https://www.wireshark.org/docs/dfref/i/ip.html), [icmp](https://www.wireshark.org/docs/dfref/i/icmp.html), [dns](https://www.wireshark.org/docs/dfref/d/dns.html), [tls](https://www.wireshark.org/docs/dfref/t/tls.html), [vxlan](https://www.wireshark.org/docs/dfref/v/vxlan.html), [geneve](https://www.wireshark.org/docs/dfref/g/geneve.html)\\n- [pcap-filter(7)](https://www.tcpdump.org/manpages/pcap-filter.7.html) and [tcpdump(1)](https://www.tcpdump.org/manpages/tcpdump.1.html) for capture filters\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 1. Method: how an expert works a capture\\n\\n1. **Pin down the capture point before reading a single packet.** Wireshark itself warns that\\n   interpretations \"may be different whether the capture was performed server side, client side\\n   or anywhere in the middle\". Ask where it was taken, or infer it (step 4).\\n2. **Treat Expert Info as a hint, not a verdict.** Per the User\\'s Guide: \"Expert information is\\n   the starting point for investigation, not the stopping point... absence of expert information\\n   doesn\\'t necessarily mean everything is OK.\"\\n3. **Get the overview first** (`-q` suppresses per-packet output):\\n   ```\\n   tshark -r cap.pcapng -q -z io,phs              # protocol hierarchy\\n   tshark -r cap.pcapng -q -z conv,tcp            # TCP conversations (bytes, duration)\\n   tshark -r cap.pcapng -q -z endpoints,ip\\n   tshark -r cap.pcapng -q -z expert,note         # expert items of severity note and above\\n   ```\\n4. **Locate the capture point with the iRTT split** [heuristic, standard practice]. In a\\n   complete handshake, SYN to SYN-ACK is the round trip from the capture point to the server,\\n   and SYN-ACK to ACK is the round trip to the client. Whichever leg is tiny is the side the\\n   capture sits next to. `tcp.analysis.initial_rtt` gives the total. Compute the split from\\n   the `frame.time_relative` values of the SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK.\\n   **No handshake in the capture?** Estimate it instead [Heuristic]:\\n   - **Round trip to the receiver:** the time from a data segment to the ACK that covers it, at\\n     the capture point.\\n   - **Round trip to the sender:** how old the `TSecr` a sender echoes is, compared with the\\n     peer\\'s current `TSval`. Check the timestamp tick rate against frame times first (it\\'s often\\n     1 ms per tick). This is approximate: the echo can lag by a tick or two.\\n   - **Hop count:** received TTL below a common starting value (64, 128 or 255) estimates hops.\\n     A host\\'s *own* outbound packets carry the starting TTL, and with offload they also show\\n     `tcp.options.mss.exceeded` or `tcp.checksum.partial`. If neither side shows those, the\\n     capture probably wasn\\'t taken on either host.\\n5. **Isolate the failing stream** (`tcp.stream == N`). Then read it in time order with\\n   `tcp.time_delta` (time since the previous frame in this TCP stream) to find the stall.\\n6. **Explain every flagged packet in context.** One retransmission doesn\\'t make a diagnosis; a\\n   pattern does, such as RTO-style retransmits after silence, or loss limited to large segments.\\n7. **Prove it from the other side when you can.** A two-sided capture turns \"probably dropped\"\\n   into \"left A, never reached B\".\\n\\n## 2. Wireshark TCP analysis flags (the core vocabulary)\\n\\nWireshark tracks each TCP session and flags problems under \"SEQ/ACK analysis\". The analysis\\nruns once per packet, in packet-list order, when the file is opened. The \"Analyze TCP sequence\\nnumbers\" preference toggles it. Filter on any flag with `tcp.analysis.<name>`, or on all of\\nthem with `tcp.analysis.flags`.\\n\\nDefinitions are paraphrased from the User\\'s Guide. \"Next expected seq\" means the last-seen seq\\nplus the segment length.\\n\\n| Filter | Set when (Wireshark definition, abridged) | What it usually means |\\n|---|---|---|\\n| `tcp.analysis.retransmission` | Not a keep-alive; length > 0 or SYN/FIN; next expected seq > this seq | The sender resent data it had already sent. After a pause, it\\'s an RTO: loss with no dup-ACK recovery. SYN retransmissions mean no reply to the SYN. |\\n| `tcp.analysis.fast_retransmission` | As above, plus at least 2 dup ACKs in reverse (or more than 2 MSS jumped), seq = next expected ack, last ACK seen < 20 ms ago. **Supersedes** Out-Of-Order and Retransmission. | Loss detected by the receiver via dup ACKs. Recovery is quicker than RTO. |\\n| `tcp.analysis.spurious_retransmission` | Length > 0, no SYN/FIN, not keep-alive, data already ACKed by the reverse direction. **Supersedes** Fast Retransmission, Out-Of-Order and Retransmission. | Unnecessary resend: the sender didn\\'t see the ACK in time (ACK loss or delay, or RTO too short). |\\n| `tcp.analysis.out_of_order` | Next expected seq > this seq, the segment\\'s next seq differs from it, and it arrived within the iRTT (default 3 ms if no iRTT). **Supersedes** Retransmission. | Reordering, for example across parallel paths. Ambiguous with fast retransmission; see the preferences in section 3. |\\n| `tcp.analysis.lost_segment` | This seq > next expected seq (\"Previous segment not captured\") | A hole before this packet. It\\'s loss upstream of the capture point **or** the capture missed it. \"Common at capture start\". |\\n| `tcp.analysis.ack_lost_segment` | This ACK > next expected ack for the reverse direction (\"ACKed unseen segment\") | The receiver ACKed data the capture never saw. **The capture missed packets.** This is not evidence of network loss. |\\n| `tcp.analysis.duplicate_ack` | Length 0; window non-zero and unchanged (or valid SACK); connection established; no SYN/FIN/RST | The receiver is still waiting for a missing segment. `tcp.analysis.duplicate_ack_num` is the count. |\\n| `tcp.analysis.keep_alive` | Length 0 or 1; seq = next expected - 1; no SYN/FIN/RST. **Supersedes** all retransmission types and Out-Of-Order. | A keepalive probe. Normal, and useful evidence of idle periods. |\\n| `tcp.analysis.keep_alive_ack` | Length 0; window unchanged; seq/ack unchanged; the previous reverse packet was a keep-alive. **Supersedes** Dup ACK and ZeroWindowProbeAck. | The peer is alive |\\n| `tcp.analysis.zero_window` | Receive window 0, no SYN/FIN/RST | **The receiver is full.** In most cases it\\'s a performance or capacity problem on the receiving end. Resuming can take a long time. |\\n| `tcp.analysis.zero_window_probe` | seq = next expected, length 1, last reverse window was 0 | The sender probing a closed window |\\n| `tcp.analysis.zero_window_probe_ack` | Length 0, window 0, seq/ack unchanged, the previous reverse packet was a probe. **Supersedes** Dup ACK. | The window is still closed |\\n| `tcp.analysis.window_full` | Segment size exceeds the reverse direction\\'s window | The sender is limited by the receiver\\'s window, which is often too small for the bandwidth-delay product |\\n| `tcp.analysis.window_update` | Length 0; window non-zero and changed; seq/ack unchanged; no SYN/FIN/RST | The receiver opened its window. After a zero window, this marks the recovery point. |\\n| `tcp.analysis.reused_ports` | SYN (not SYN+ACK) for an existing conversation with a different ISN | Port reuse. It\\'s only a problem if a middlebox (NAT, conntrack) still holds the old state. |\\n\\n**Counting: flags can overlap.** \"Supersedes\" in the User\\'s Guide describes how Wireshark\\nclassifies a packet, but it does **not** mean a packet carries only one filter flag. Verified on\\ntshark 4.6.9: a spurious retransmission carries **both** `tcp.analysis.spurious_retransmission`\\nand `tcp.analysis.retransmission`, with two expert items on the same frame. So:\\n- `tcp.analysis.retransmission` counts include spurious ones. For \"real\" (RTO-style) resends,\\n  use `tcp.analysis.retransmission && !tcp.analysis.spurious_retransmission`.\\n- For \"all resends\", filter on `tcp.analysis.retransmission || tcp.analysis.fast_retransmission`.\\n  Don\\'t add the spurious count on top, or you\\'ll double-count.\\n- **Out-of-order segments do not** also carry `tcp.analysis.retransmission`. That was verified\\n  on 22 out-of-order segments in 4 Wireshark test captures (tshark 4.6.9); each had only its\\n  own expert message.\\n- Whether **fast retransmissions** also carry `tcp.analysis.retransmission` hasn\\'t been checked\\n  against a real capture (none of the example-public captures contained one). - **"ACKed segment that wasn't captured"** (`tcp.analysis.ack_lost_segment`) fires when the receiver ACKs data your capture never saw. Per Wireshark's own documentation, this means *the capture missed packets* — it is not evidence of network loss.
- **"Previous segment not captured"** (`tcp.analysis.lost_segment`) just means there's a sequence-number hole before that packet. It's ambiguous between network loss and capture loss on its own.
